newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajik fighter to free hostages, sets new demands.
newsitem.headline: Tajik fighter to free hostages, sets new demands.

text.p: Tajik hostage-taker Bakhrom Sadirov says he will free five of his captives on Thursday, but will step up his demands unless a previous ultimatum is met, according to a statement from the United Nations in Dushanbe.
The U.N. said it had received a message from Sadirov. "He wishes it to be disseminated as widely and as quickly as possible," the U.N. said.
Sadirov's own statement said he would release four Russian journalists and one U.N. representative unconditionally.

But he said his demands that 40 fighters be allowed into Tajikistan had not been met and he set a new deadline of four p.m. (1100 GMT) on Thursday for them to arrive. If this did not happen he would insist that 136 fighters be allowed in.

"Commander Bakhrom has shown remarkable patience which proves his positive attitude; however, should the Tajik government delay the ultimatum given, he would be forced to set a new ultimatum," the message said.

Sadirov's men are holding four U.N. military observers, four Russian reporters, four workers with the United Nations refugee agency and Tajikistan's Security Minister, who was seized when he flew in to negotiate.
There have been a series of announcements that the hostages would be released, but none has been fulfilled.

The Tajik government is struggling to assert its authority against armed groups across the impoverished former Soviet republic. Many Islamic fighters -- like the rest of Sadirov's group -- are based in neighbouring Afghanistan.
The authorities sent helicopters to Afghanistan to pick up Sadirov's 40 fighters on Wednesday, but government officials said the return flight had been delayed for technical reasons.

Sadirov's brother, rebel leader Rizvon Sadirov, returned from Afghanistan on Monday to help negotiate the release of the hostages. Rizvon Sadirov is now reported to be at his brother's base near the town of Obigarm in a mountainous area 80 km (50 miles) east of Dushanbe.
The hostage crisis comes as the government and the opposition rebels are trying to end a bitter four-year civil war that has left tens of thousands dead and many more homeless.
A ceasefire agreed at a meeting in northern Afghanistan last December appears to be holding.
